skript.thema: Gemini 4 Carbon: what it costs, who can use it, and when paying is worth it

teile.text: I read one pricing line, and one word scared me. Gemini 4 Carbon is built to hunt software flaws, and most of us can't even use it yet. But the bug I mean isn't in code.
teile.szene: Painted urban open-world-game poster style: a black-haired man in a black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses stands on a rainy rooftop at night, frowning at a flickering city skyline, medium shot, neon rim light.

teile.text: Here's the question this video answers. What does Carbon cost, who can use it, and when is paying actually worth it? The announcement headline calls it our next frontier model.
teile.szene: Source card showing the announcement headline 'Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model' and the subhead about state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities, calm margins above and below.

teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted urban game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man in a black leather jacket leans on a graffiti-covered wall at dusk, warm smile, one hand raised in a friendly gesture, medium shot, soft streetlight.

teile.name: Who gets Carbon
teile.text: Start with the rollout paragraph. It says that starting this week, Google will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the rollout paragraph: 'Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders', passage emphasized, calm margins.

teile.text: Cyber defenders are the people who protect systems from attackers. The same paragraph names the Fairwind Program, which will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the phrase 'gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program', calm margins.

teile.text: Developers, businesses and consumers come after that. The page says Google is still gathering feedback and iterating on guardrails before offering Carbon through its product surfaces as soon as possible.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: a crowd of anonymous people queue patiently outside a closed shop door in a city street at golden hour, wide shot, the cyan-glasses man at the back checking his watch.

teile.text: The page calls this a deliberate approach, and says Google is actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout' and 'voluntary process for pre-release model testing', calm margins.

teile.text: Here's the catch. The page gives no date for wider access. Artificial Analysis, an outside tracking site, says Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available.
teile.szene: Source card of the Artificial Analysis article passage 'is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available', emphasized, calm margins.

teile.name: The price
teile.text: So why look at the price at all? Find the pricing paragraph. One word in it is the budget bug I promised.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man leans toward a shop counter in a night market, narrowing his eyes with suspicion, medium shot, warm lantern light.

teile.text: The sentence reads: Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price as Argon. Argon is Google's earlier model, launched two weeks before this announcement.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the sentence 'Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price as Argon', calm margins.

teile.text: The figures are $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. A token is a small chunk of text. Input is what you send. Output is what comes back.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting '$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens', calm margins.

teile.text: The same sentence adds that cached input tokens are priced at 95% off the input token price.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price', calm margins.

teile.text: Now look at the word introductory. Google's page doesn't say how long that price lasts. Budgets prefer the word permanent.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man in a leather jacket squints skeptically with one eyebrow raised in a dim diner booth, close medium shot, warm lamp light.

teile.text: Artificial Analysis adds context. Its pricing bullet says $4 and $20 per million input and output tokens, with a 50% discount. It says that launch discount has no confirmed end date.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the Pricing bullet: '$4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens... with a 50% discount', and 'no confirmed end date', calm margins.

teile.text: Half of $4 and $20 is $2 and $10, so the two pages line up. Still, Artificial Analysis is an outside site, so check Google's own line before you budget.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man at a workbench counting on his fingers, thoughtful, two small coffee cups beside him, medium shot, warm side light.

teile.text: What about a free version? The announcement lists a price and a rollout plan. It never mentions a free tier for Carbon, so we won't promise one.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man shrugs with open empty hands at a quiet street market stall, medium shot, soft overcast light.

teile.text: Free access, downloadable weights and commercial rights are three different things. The launch-price sentence promises none of them. Only token prices are written down.
teile.szene: Source card showing the launch-price sentence with token prices highlighted, calm margins.

teile.name: What it's for
teile.text: So what would you be paying for? Look at the headline pitch: state-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems. That's where the page spends most of its numbers.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the heading 'State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems', calm margins.

teile.text: Under it come three steps: vulnerability detection, validation and remediation. A vulnerability is a software flaw an attacker could abuse. Remediation means fixing it.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: an anonymous locksmith kneels at a worn warehouse door, inspecting a crack in the frame with a flashlight, close medium shot, dramatic side light.

teile.text: The Multimodality bullet on the outside site lists text, image, video and speech input, with text output. So Carbon accepts more than text, but it writes text back.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the Multimodality bullet 'Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output', calm margins.

teile.text: SEC-bench Pro is the first benchmark. The page gives Carbon 88.2% for finding real vulnerabilities, and says it autonomously uncovered complex flaws buried in real-world software.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro', calm margins.

teile.text: ExploitGym is second, at 54.8%. The page ties it to checking which vulnerabilities are actually exploitable, so defenders know what to remediate first.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Validating risk through exploitation' and 'ExploitGym (54.8%)', calm margins.

teile.text: CWE-bench, from Collinear, is third, at 71.0%. The page describes that as turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Note the number: 71.0%, not 100%.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Patching at the root cause' and 'Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear's CWE-bench', calm margins.

teile.text: Now read the caption above those three scores: evaluated without guardrails. Guardrails are safety limits. These are test scores, not results on your own code.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails)', calm margins.

teile.text: One claim on that page goes straight at everyday coding, and it comes with a multiplier.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man in a leather jacket sits typing at a laptop seen from behind his shoulder, café window at night, medium shot, cyan reflections on his glasses.

teile.text: The page says Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. Internal benchmarks means Google's own tests.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon', calm margins.

teile.text: The Chrome team gets a mention too. The page says it reported Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model at generating high quality patches. A patch is a code fix.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better' ... 'generating high quality patches', calm margins.

teile.text: Wiz, which the page calls Google's leading cloud security platform, is quoted as well. It observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, for its Scan for Good initiative.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Wiz' and 'Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing' and 'Scan for Good initiative', calm margins.

teile.name: The honest numbers
teile.text: Now the outside view. Artificial Analysis puts Carbon number 1 on its Intelligence Index v5, with 59. It holds the top score in 4 of 9 evaluations, but not in coding and knowledge work.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting headline 'Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5' and the '4 of the 9 Index evaluations' bullet, calm margins.

teile.text: On its Coding Agent Index, Carbon scores 59. Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 scores 62. So for coding agents, Carbon is second.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents' bullet with scores 59 and 62, calm margins.

teile.text: Another bullet covers AA-Briefcase, an agentic knowledge work test. Carbon scores 1609 Elo, up 126 over Argon, but still behind Grok 4.7, Muse Wonder and Kimi K3.1 Pro.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading' with 1609 Elo and the 126-point improvement, calm margins.

teile.text: Would cheaper per task settle it? Find the cost line. Cost per Intelligence Index task is $7.76 at standard pricing, about 23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 at $10.04.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the bullet 'Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5' with $7.76 and $10.04, calm margins.

teile.text: The same bullet lists GPT-6 Astra at $6.25 per task. So cheaper than one rival isn't cheapest. Carbon uses 123k output tokens per task, versus 173k for Claude Opus 5.5.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25)' and 'It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5', calm margins.

teile.text: Cheap answers only help if they're right. Open the AA-Omniscience bullet, because one number there went the wrong way.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man stands at a crossroads in a neon-lit alley, looking down one path then another, wide shot, wet pavement reflections.

teile.text: Accuracy rises 10 points over Argon, to 58%. But the hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the bullet 'Leading AA-Omniscience v1.1 score, with low hallucination' with accuracy 58% and hallucination rate 4% to 11%, calm margins.

teile.text: A hallucination is when a model states something false as fact. The page says 11% is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra both sit at 50%.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon, compared with 50% for both Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max)', calm margins.

teile.text: Back on Google's page, there's a bigger promise about long jobs. It says internally, teams have seen Carbon run for days on tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends' and 'root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases', calm margins.

teile.text: A job running for days invites a fear of shortcuts. Under the heading Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation, the page reports successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 0.0%, with attempts at 0.4%.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation' and 'reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%', calm margins.

teile.text: It also says high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80% in live coding environments with internal teams. Misalignment means the model behaving in ways you didn't intend. That's Google's own observation.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%', calm margins.

teile.text: The safety section names a multi-layered stack: model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience and chain-of-thought monitoring. Prompt injection means hidden instructions slipped into text the model reads.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'multi-layered safety and security stack' with 'model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring', calm margins.

teile.text: Under Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity, the page says Carbon surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting. Under Greater transparency and honesty, it says unsupported claims are cut by approximately 2x over Argon.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity' and 'Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon', calm margins.

teile.name: Is paying worth it
teile.text: So when would paying be worth it? The page's own focus is the clearest hint: the cybersecurity defense lifecycle, from vulnerability detection through remediation.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man in a leather jacket walks along a bright city bridge at dawn, determined, wide shot, warm sunrise light.

teile.text: Hypothetically, say you maintain a small web app full of old code. Finding a flaw, checking it's real, and fixing it is the three-step job the page describes.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: a hypothetical small-app maintainer, the cyan-glasses man, sits in a cluttered workshop surrounded by stacked old cardboard boxes, studying one box carefully, medium shot, warm lamp light.

teile.text: Hypothetically again, you only need a quick page layout. The page notes Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at number 4, 1768, on WebDev Arena. That's a ranking, not a price tag.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena', calm margins.

teile.text: Check the launch prices once more. Output costs five times input, so a job that writes a lot costs more than one that mostly reads. Cached input is priced 95% off, so repeated input costs less per token.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting '$2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off', calm margins.

teile.text: So here's the hidden budget bug. It's that one word, introductory. Google's page doesn't say how long the price lasts, and the outside site builds its charts on standard pricing of $4 and $20.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting 'All our charts and figures use standard pricing' and 'Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date', calm margins.

teile.text: Right now, access starts with cyber defenders and trusted partners. For most of us, paying isn't an option yet, and the announcement lists no free tier for Carbon.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man in a black leather jacket stands at a city overlook at golden hour, calm and resolved, wide shot, glowing cyan glasses catching the light.

teile.text: When access opens, check three lines: the token price, the cost per task and the hallucination rate. Those are the numbers on these pages that touch your wallet and your trust.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man counts three fingers up in front of a mural-covered wall, expressive, medium shot, soft daylight.

teile.text: Quick recap. Carbon claims 88.2% on finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on exploitation and 71.0% on patching, at an introductory $2 and $10. These are documented scores, not our results.
teile.szene: Source card highlighting the three benchmark lines SEC-bench Pro 88.2%, ExploitGym 54.8%, CWE-bench 71.0%, calm margins.

teile.text: So the budget bug was never in the code. It was one word on a pricing line. Whether you can hire Carbon waits on Google's rollout. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses man in a black leather jacket sits relaxed on a rooftop edge at sunrise, city waking below, a quiet smile, wide shot, warm light.

skript.beschreibung: Gemini 4 Carbon's announced introductory price, limited rollout and secure-coding benchmark claims, plus what an outside tracker says about cost per task. Figures come from Google's announcement and Artificial Analysis.

belege.name: Gemini 4 Carbon
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (1019 points, 2026-10-28).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model
Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google
Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.
Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.
We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.
Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price
as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.
Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks
Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.
Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena .
State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems
Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.
Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):
Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.
Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%).
Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.
Advancing frontier model safety & security
Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.
Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.
Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.
Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.
Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 2

belege.name: Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (339 points, 2026-10-29).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 | Artificial Analysis
Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 See model page
Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index
Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on Intelligence Index v5, driven by leading performance in complex reasoning, knowledge, and scientific tasks. It also has large gains in coding and knowledge work, particularly when compared to other Gemini models, but it is not leading in all these areas.
As with launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available. Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date. All our charts and figures use standard pricing for both Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon.
Key results for Gemini 4 Carbon with high reasoning:
➤ Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index v5, with the #1 score in 4 of the 9 Index evaluations: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon makes substantial gains elsewhere but is not leading in coding and knowledge work
➤ Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 59 only 3 points behind Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Carbon ranks second on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) and FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), behind Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 56%. Google has historically underperformed in this area and so this improvement stands out.
➤ Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading: On AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 1609 Elo, a 126-point improvement over Gemini 4 Argon (high, 1483), but still behind models including Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). The largest gain comes from Presentation, up 293 Elo to 1598, alongside a 120-point improvement in Analytical Quality to 1671
➤ Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5 for comparable overall intelligence: With standard pricing, Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25).
